extracted.intended_audience: college students or general readers studying American government, criminal law, and municipal government
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook guidance describing substantive criminal-law definitions and criminal-procedure rules, together with principles and institutional arrangements governing municipal government and home rule. Intended to teach what constitutes crimes, how criminal trials proceed, and how cities relate to state legislatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of crimes: felonies and misdemeanors
rubrics_metrics.description: All crimes are divided into two classes; felonies and misdemeanors. The former includes graver offences (generally punished by death or confinement in a state's prison); the latter includes lesser offences ordinarily punished by fines or short imprisonment in a penitentiary or county jail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the broad rule for classifying offences and explains that specific offences may be placed in either category by statute; conviction of a felony often carries collateral consequences (e.g., loss of right to vote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal felonies and their elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal felonies named are murder, manslaughter, arson, burglary, robbery, and larceny, each defined by their characteristic elements (e.g., murder = intentional killing; manslaughter = unintentional killing; arson = wilful and malicious burning of a dwelling-house).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives concrete examples to distinguish these offences (e.g., negligent killing by automobile as manslaughter; slight incendiarism suffices for arson). Notes that some crimes are subdivided into degrees based on premeditation or other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Murder vs manslaughter (degrees, intent, heat of passion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Murder is intentional killing; manslaughter is unintentional killing. Murder is sometimes divided into degrees according to premeditation; intentional killing in sudden heat of passion caused by adequate provocation is generally regarded as manslaughter, not murder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides examples (accidental death from negligent driving, railroad wreck, or a blow not intended to kill) and explains that degrees and provocation affect classification and punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arson definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Arson is willful and malicious burning of a dwelling-house; any incendiarism, however slight, is sufficient to constitute the crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that the offense focuses on malicious burning and that the dwelling-house element is important in the common-law definition given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burglary definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Burglary consists in breaking and entering into the house of another with the express intention of committing some felony therein; the breaking and entering itself is burglary whether or not a further felony is actually committed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stresses the mens rea (intent to commit felony inside) and the actus reus (breaking and entering), and that completion of an additional crime is unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robbery vs larceny distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Robbery is taking another's property from his person or in his presence by force. Picking a man's pocket so he is unaware is larceny, not robbery; taking money at the point of a pistol or knocking a person down then stealing from him is robbery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides classification by whether force or presence-of-victim elements are present; provides examples to distinguish thefts categorized as robbery versus larceny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Larceny and gradation by amount
rubrics_metrics.description: Larceny is stealing the personal property of another. Various forms of theft and swindling fall under larceny and it is often divided into grand and petty larceny according to the amount stolen (grand being a felony, petty a misdemeanor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how value thresholds affect classification and punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other named felonies (forgery, counterfeiting, kidnapping, bigamy, perjury)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many other offences are often made felonies: forgery (making or altering a written instrument to defraud), counterfeiting (false money — federal offense), kidnapping, bigamy (having more than one spouse simultaneously), and perjury (wilful giving of false testimony under oath).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives typical statutory examples and notes federal jurisdiction for some crimes (counterfeiting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Misdemeanors and miscellaneous minor offences
rubrics_metrics.description: Other offences (varying by state) are misdemeanors: mayhem (usually misdemeanor), bribery (sometimes felony), receiving stolen goods, malicious libel (defamation in print), assault and battery, disturbance of the peace, violations of food laws, misuse of weights and measures, spitting on public conveyances, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates the broad category of minor offences and their variety across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempt to commit a crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishment may be inflicted for the attempt to commit a crime when a person conceives the design and takes some steps toward carrying it out but is prevented from effecting it. A less punishment is inflicted for an unsuccessful attempt than for the completed crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: shooting at someone with intent to kill but missing constitutes an attempt to commit murder; emphasizes partial culpability and reduced punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accomplices: accessories before and after the fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Principals and their accomplices are punishable; accomplices before the fact are those who advise, encourage, or assist in preparation and may be punished as principals; accessories after the fact assist escape or help cover up the crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that in some states accessories before the fact are placed with principals for punishment; distinguishes roles and timing of assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of criminal intent and excuses/defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: To be convicted a person must have criminal intent; intent is ordinarily presumed but certain categories (small children, insane persons) lack such intent and are not responsible. Legal tests of insanity are stricter than medical tests. Voluntary intoxication is not an excuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies which mental-state defenses are recognized and the burden of law versus medicine; emphasizes intoxication is generally not a defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution in the name of the state and initiation of criminal proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal prosecutions are conducted by a prosecuting officer in the name of the state. A criminal proceeding ordinarily begins with the arrest of the offender, either by warrant or without warrant in certain circumstances (crime committed in view, reasonable grounds to believe a felony was committed and the arrestee committed it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains arrest rules vary by state and gives the principal common-law bases for warrantless arrests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magistrate examination and accused's right not to be questioned
rubrics_metrics.description: After arrest the accused is brought before a magistrate who examines the case and hears evidence; neither at this examination nor at subsequent stages may the accused be questioned unless he himself desires to testify — a cardinal principle distinguishing Anglo‑American procedure from continental European practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights the accused's privilege against compulsion to testify and contrasts with inquisitorial systems; mentions abuses (third-degree practices) that violate these principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bail and sureties; exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a magistrate finds probable cause, he commits the accused to jail but allows bail unless the accusation is murder. Bail means one or two sureties sign a bond obligating payment if the accused fails to appear; if bail is given the person is released.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes amount varies with enormity of offence and probability of escape; procedural explanation of effect of bail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indictment by grand jury: probable cause, secrecy, and majority rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The grand jury (historic common-law body) examines accusations presented by the prosecuting attorney and finds an indictment if sufficient evidence exists which, if unrebutted, will probably convict. Proceedings are secret, the grand jury hears only the prosecution, and a majority vote (not unanimous) is sufficient to indict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains grand jury's role as safeguard against oppressive prosecutions, its ability to investigate on its own, and that indictment allows the case to proceed to trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information as alternative to grand jury (prosecutorial control)
rubrics_metrics.description: In some states indictment by grand jury is unnecessary; prosecution may proceed by 'information' — an accusation brought by the prosecuting attorney. This gives more influence to the prosecutor, who then has sole power to determine whether to bring a case to trial; generally used for minor offences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts grand-jury secrecy with prosecutorial information filing and notes its typical limited use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arraignment, pleas, and immediate consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: After indictment the accused is arraigned, the charge read, and he is directed to plead. If he pleads guilty, the judge imposes sentence with no further proceedings (except for some serious offences like first-degree murder where trial form must be employed); if not guilty, the case proceeds to trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets out implicated procedural consequences of plea choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial process: jury selection, impartiality, and peremptory challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: At trial a jury of twelve men is impanelled; jurors are examined (voir dire) by both sides and any juror with a definite opinion on the case is incompetent. Each side may challenge a certain number peremptorily without stating a reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that selection can be lengthy, especially in sensational cases, and gives practical examples of delay and expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of evidence, cross-examination, and rules of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution opens and calls witnesses; defendant may cross-examine after each direct. Questions are limited by rules of evidence so irrelevant matter is excluded and witnesses confined to facts they know. Objections are decided by the judge, and dissatisfaction is preserved by taking an 'exception.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes protective purpose of evidence rules (to prevent jury being misled) and outlines objection/exception practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accused's right not to testify and consequences of testifying
rubrics_metrics.description: The prisoner is not questioned at trial unless he chooses to testify; if he does take the stand, the prosecution may cross-examine him like any other witness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reiterates privilege against compelled testimony and strategic implications of choosing to testify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge's charge, elements of crime, and standard of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: After closing speeches the judge charges the jury — sums up evidence, states the law applying to the case, tells jurors what must be shown to constitute the crime and describes degrees and how much proof is necessary. The jury must be convinced 'beyond a reasonable doubt' to convict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights the centrality of the judge's charge in framing legal issues and instructing on the burden of proof standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury deliberation, unanimity, and hung juries
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurors retire to deliberate and must, as a rule, arrive at a unanimous verdict, which can take many hours. If absolutely unable to agree they are discharged (hung jury) and the prisoner must be tried again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes some states permit non-unanimous verdicts in certain cases (e.g., nine or ten jurors allowed in some Western states).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentencing: punishment types and judicial discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishment for most crimes is imprisonment; fines are common for minor offences; sentences vary from short confinement to imprisonment at hard labor for life. Law generally prescribes minimum and maximum limits; trial judge has discretion to impose punishment within those limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentions cruel practices (chain-gangs) and historical context; notes possibility of gubernatorial pardon and reduction for good behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indeterminate sentence and probation
rubrics_metrics.description: Indeterminate sentence: judge imposes minimum and maximum terms and release between those depends on behavior and promise of reform. Early release is often accompanied by probation and reporting requirements to prison officials or probation officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains rehabilitative rationale and mechanisms for conditional release and supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital punishment: methods, abolition, and critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: For murder the death penalty is inflicted in most states; execution usually by hanging, though electrocution has been substituted in some states. A few states have abolished capital punishment. Opponents argue fear of death does not diminish crime rates, juries may avoid convicting when penalty is death, and the risk of executing the innocent conflicts with reformation goals of punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes empirical and moral arguments against capital punishment and notes risk of miscarriage of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of appeal and grounds for reversal
rubrics_metrics.description: After conviction the prisoner may appeal to higher tribunals for mistakes made by the trial judge. Alleged errors in admission/exclusion of evidence or incorrect statement of law in the judge's charge are grounds for reversal. Successful appeal typically results in a new trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes reversals for prejudicial errors from those for purely technical errors; notes appellate practice should refuse reversal if errors could not have prejudiced the defendant in the eyes of the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concerns about liberal appeals and procedural delays
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism exists that liberal systems of appeals in criminal and civil procedure cause delays and occasional failure of justice; many reversals are for technical reasons that may not have injured the defendant, yet some reversals correct obvious injustices (e.g., wrongfully excluded defense evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides statistics and examples (e.g., low appeal rates and success rates in New York County 1898–1902) and recommends appellate restraint and better trial control to reduce delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial-judge control to reduce delays and technical reversals
rubrics_metrics.description: Many delays and technicalities of legal procedure can be avoided if trial judges exercise greater control over the proceedings (as in England and to a lesser extent in federal courts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates for proactive judicial management to minimize grounds for appeal and procedural inefficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Position of the city relative to the state (charter and legislative control)
rubrics_metrics.description: The American city (in most commonwealths) is largely subject to the state legislature, which creates its charter, establishes form of government, fixes powers, and can from time to time impose new institutions on top of those in the charter. Thus cities are largely at the mercy of the legislature, unless protected by constitutional provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames the institutional baseline that motivates the municipal 'home rule' debate; highlights how state politics and rural-majority constitutional discrimination can affect cities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal home rule: arguments for practical autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Champions of municipal home rule argue state legislatures are unfitted to control matters affecting only urban dwellers because they lack time, knowledge, and responsibility to urban constituencies; rural-majority representation can impose unsuited laws on cities; purely municipal problems (paving, lighting, transportation, waterworks, markets) should be left to municipal voters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets out the practical and democratic rationales for decentralization and local autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments against unlimited municipal home rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Reply: few municipal functions are without general state interest (e.g., waterworks often require state concessions for watersheds; transportation systems and public health affect broader regions), commerce and industry have become state concerns, and it is impossible to arbitrarily fix the boundary between state and municipal interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites historical development (Goodnow) and examples (Massachusetts water-supply competition, Chicago sewage using interstate rivers vs. New York discharging into ocean) to show interdependence and limits of home rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for limits on state legislature power over municipalities and institutional responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite state interest, abuses by state legislatures require some check on their control; several plans have been devised to address the problem (constitutional provisions, classifications, mayoral approval requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduces concrete institutional reforms discussed in subsequent sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional prohibition on special local laws (Pennsylvania 1873 example) and its limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Pennsylvania's 1873 constitutional rule forbade state legislature from passing local or special laws regulating counties, cities, etc., but this proved too narrow as the legislature later passed laws targeted at cities above a population threshold and courts construed the prohibition narrowly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the practical difficulty of rigid constitutional bans on special legislation and judicial responses that preserved legislative flexibility for necessary governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and local approval for special laws (New York model)
rubrics_metrics.description: New York classified cities into groups by population and required that special laws (affecting a single city or fewer than all cities of a class) be transmitted to the city's mayor (for first-class cities approval is required) or mayor and city council, before becoming law; if not approved locally, the bill may be repassed by the originating branch of the legislature by ordinary majority to become law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents a practical compromise giving cities a voice in special legislation via local executive or council approval and a legislative override mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: State interest examples making municipal matters state concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: city waterworks may require control over watersheds outside municipal boundaries; municipal transportation systems often serve areas beyond city limits; sewage disposal may involve state waterways — thus municipal functions often have state or even national implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses concrete geographic and infrastructural examples (New York, Chicago) to show why municipal actions implicate broader state interests and complicate pure home rule.
